## The decision tree

**If L=32, T=T_c jsLoss beats reverse-KL's floor (KL_qp drops well below 12):**
→ YES, sweep JS over T. JS would be a real architectural fix, and mapping its T-dependence vs forward-KL's would reveal whether the symmetric loss helps everywhere or only near criticality.

**If L=32, T=T_c jsLoss just trades one error for the other (KL_qp up, KL_pq down, sum ~= existing forward-KL):**
→ SKIP the sweep. JS is then just an interpolation; off-critical T's won't show anything new (at T<<T_c modes are weakly bimodal, at T>>T_c the target is single-peaked → JS reduces to either KL alone).

## Why I'd wait

Off-critical points are exactly where JS *can't* help in principle:
- T=2.15 (below T_c): broad single-mode dominance per direction; reverse-KL behaves fine
- T=2.40 (above T_c): single-peak Gaussian-like target; JS = forward-KL = reverse-KL essentially
- T=2.269 (at T_c): bimodal, critical fluctuations, mode-dropping is sharpest — **this is where JS's symmetry matters most**

So T_c is the cleanest test bed. A full sweep would only be informative if T_c already showed gain.

## If you want to commit anyway: cheapest version

**L=8 jsLoss sweep only** (5 T points) — costs ~5h total parallel on preempt:
- L=8 forward-KL sweep already done → directly comparable
- Cheap insurance — if JS does help, you get curves immediately
- L=16 sweep adds little (mid-size); L=32 should wait for the anchor decision anyway

Hold for ~3-4 more hours until anchor `38774030` converges. The L_rev / L_fwd component breakdown in its log will tell us in one number whether the sweep is worth it.

In the meantime the diagnostic sweep results will land, giving us the T_c-shift answer from forward-KL data (the existing sweep) — that's a separate, complete story that doesn't need JS.

## Problem Statement

Training MERA-based normalizing flows (NeuralRG) on the 2D Ising model (L=32) near the critical temperature T_c ≈ 2.269. Two training modes are available:

## Read

**JS did NOT break the mode-dropping floor at L=32.** It actually pushed KL(q‖p) up (12 → 17) — by spending gradient on the forward term, the optimizer relaxed the reverse-KL minimization. In exchange, KL(p‖q) improved over the default-arch forward-KL.

This is **the "just trades errors" outcome** I described in the decision rule. Strict per-direction comparisons:
- Worse than pure reverse-KL in the q‖p direction
- Better than pure forward-KL in the p‖q direction
- Worse than bignet capacity in either direction

The one genuine win: **JS bounds BOTH errors** symmetrically (~17 / 16 nat). Neither pure baseline does that — reverse-KL has KL(p‖q)≈89 (mode-dropped), forward-KL has KL(q‖p)≈20 (over-coherent). So if you want a flow whose worst-case directional KL is bounded, JS at the same arch as either is a 2-3× improvement on the worst direction.

## Sweep decision: SKIP the L=32 jsLoss T-sweep

Per the criterion set earlier: JS didn't break the floor (KL_qp went up not down), so the T-sweep wouldn't tell us much new. Off-T_c the bimodality weakens and JS becomes redundant.

Two narrower follow-ups that would still be informative if you want to push JS:
1. **L=32 jsLoss BIGNET** (16/128, 5k epochs): same combo but with capacity to actually satisfy both terms simultaneously. Predicted to land around KL_qp ~5-8 and KL_pq ~5-8 — if so, that IS a real win over either pure-bignet alone.
2. **λ-sweep at L=32 default arch**: λ ∈ {0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7} to map the Pareto front of the two KLs. Reveals the symmetric vs asymmetric tradeoff cleanly.

But for the L=32 T-sweep specifically — skip. Want me to set up either of (1) or (2), or wrap up the session here?

## Yes, converged

Smoothed L_js trajectory shows clear asymptotic saturation:

| Epoch | L_js (200-ep smoothed) | Δ from prev |
|---|---|---|
| 500 | −197.4 | — |
| 1000 | −205.0 | **−7.6** |
| 2000 | −211.4 | −6.4 |
| 3000 | −213.2 | −1.8 |
| 4000 | −214.6 | −1.4 |
| 4900 | −215.0 | **−0.4** |

Slope analysis:
- last 1000 ep: −0.37 nat / 1000 ep
- last 500 ep: −0.23 nat / 1000 ep
- **last 300 ep: +0.92 nat / 1000 ep** (drifting *up*)
- Per-epoch noise: std = 2.24 nat

The last ~1000 epochs gained only 0.4 nat, and the last 300 actually drifted up — we're in pure noise-floor regime. The gradient signal is exhausted at this capacity.

This is **qualitatively different** from `sym_bignet`, which after 2000 epochs still had a clear −0.36 nat/1000ep slope (real continued improvement). JS at default arch saturated around epoch 3000 and ran out of headroom from the model, not the budget.

## Implication

The "JS doesn't break the L=32 mode-dropping floor" conclusion is robust — not a "need more epochs" artifact. To make JS actually win, you'd need to relieve the capacity bottleneck:

- **L=32 jsLoss BIGNET** is the natural test. Each of the two KL terms wants the flow to occupy a different geometric configuration; with only 1M params (default arch) the flow can't satisfy both simultaneously, so JS forces a compromise that neither term likes. Bignet (10.9M params) should have enough capacity to drive both terms much lower in parallel.

Without that bigger-arch follow-up, the answer remains: at L=32, default arch, **JS just averages the errors** — confirms the mode-dropping is objective × capacity coupled, not pure objective.

## User <sup>5/27/2026, 11:06:38 AM</sup>

While this JS baseline elegantly balances the "mass-covering" and "mode-seeking" behaviors to prevent mode collapse, it comes with a harsh practical reality: it is computationally expensive. You lose the "data-free" elegance of pure Reverse KL because you still have to keep those 200k MCMC samples in memory. Furthermore, you are effectively doing twice the work per step—running the network both forwards and backwards—which drastically increases the time it takes to process a single epoch.

Since this approach calculates two distinct computational graphs per step, does your current implementation support running this dual-pass without hitting a massive memory bottleneck on the cluster?

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 11:07:15 AM</sup>

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 11:07:34 AM</sup>

Good question — let me audit the actual implementation rather than guess.

## What my implementation does, mechanically

```python
# Both these calls build computational graphs:
x_q, sampleLogProbability = flow.sample(batchSize)        # graph 1 (reverse)
log_q_p = flow.logProbability(x_real)                      # graph 2 (forward)

# Then:
loss = jsLambda * rev_term + (1 - jsLambda) * fwd_term
loss.backward()    # traverses BOTH graphs in one pass, frees both
```

So yes — **two graphs are alive simultaneously** until the single `loss.backward()` call. Peak GPU memory is roughly 2× a single-direction step.

## Is this hitting a bottleneck in practice?

Empirically, no — based on what's actually running:

| Run | Arch | dim | GPU | mem req | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L=8 jsLoss | 10/64 (~1M params) | 64 | l40 | 16 GB | ✓ ran to 10k ep, no issue |
| L=16 jsLoss | 10/64 | 256 | mixed | 20 GB | RUNNING fine |
| L=32 jsLoss default | 10/64 | 1024 | mixed | 24 GB | ✓ ran to 5k ep |
| L=32 jsLoss BIGNET | 16/128 (~10.9M params) | 1024 | l40 | 24 GB | RUNNING, no OOM |

The activations dominate memory pressure (params themselves are <50 MB even at bignet). At batch=128 the dual-graph footprint is well within l40's 48 GB headroom. For older P100s (16 GB) at L=32 bignet I'd be worried, but we asked for l40-class with `gpu:1` and got it.

## Where it WOULD bite

1. **Larger L** (L≥64): activations scale linearly in L²; the dual-graph holding cost could exceed l40 at bignet capacity. Would need either smaller batch or memory optimization.
2. **Larger batch**: linear in batch_size. Currently 128 is conservative.
3. **Older GPUs**: P100 (16GB), V100-16GB, T4 (16GB) — these are the marginal ones.
4. **CPU memory**: `torch.load` loads all 200k HS samples into RAM (~819MB at L=32) and keeps them there for the dataloader. Modest by cluster standards but real — pure reverse-KL has zero RAM footprint for data.

## What the implementation does NOT currently do (but could)

Gradient accumulation would halve peak GPU memory at the cost of two backward passes:

```python
flow.zero_grad()
rev_loss = jsLambda * rev_term
rev_loss.backward()        # frees graph 1 immediately
fwd_loss = (1 - jsLambda) * fwd_term
fwd_loss.backward()        # accumulates into the same .grad fields
optimizer.step()
```

Mathematically identical (gradients accumulate), but peak memory drops from "2 graphs alive" to "1 graph alive, twice." Modest speed cost (~5-10% — two kernel launches per backward instead of one). Worth implementing only if (a) we want to scale to L=64+ or (b) we move off l40-class hardware.

## TL;DR

Current implementation: **2× peak GPU memory** of a single-direction step + **CPU footprint of full HS dataset**. The "no bottleneck on cluster" check is **passing empirically** because we requested l40 with 24 GB, and 24 GB is comfortable for the dual-graph hold at L=32 bignet × batch=128. It would break for L=64 bignet at this batch size, but we have escape valves (gradient accumulation, smaller batch).

Want me to add the gradient-accumulation variant as an opt-in flag (`-jsMemOpt`)? It's a one-line change in `train/learn.py` plus the arg.

## L=8 jsLoss diagnostic — both KLs are balanced, not catastrophic in either direction

| Method | KL(q‖p) | KL(p‖q) | Sum | Worst-direction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sym` (pure reverse-KL) | **0.71** | 2.00 | 2.71 | 2.00 ← mode-drop signature |
| `hs_dataDriven` (pure forward-KL) | 0.96 | **1.35** | **2.31** | 1.35 |
| **`jsLoss` λ=0.5** | 1.36 | 1.15 | 2.51 | 1.36 |

**Structural** (flow vs data):

| Metric | jsLoss q | data p | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⟨\|M\|⟩ | 2.934 | 2.811 | **+4.4%** over |
| ξ_eff | 2.92 | 2.83 | +3.2% over |
| G(L/2)/G(0) | 0.686 | 0.654 | +4.9% over |

## Three observations

**1. JS is the only method whose two KL directions are nearly equal** (1.36 / 1.15, ratio 1.18). Pure sym has ratio 2.8 (q narrower than p), pure hs_dataDriven has ratio 0.71 (q wider than p). JS landed exactly on the symmetric Pareto point — by design.

**2. JS does NOT beat each pure method in its own direction**:
- KL(q‖p): JS 1.36 vs sym 0.71 — JS is **2× worse** in the reverse direction
- KL(p‖q): JS 1.15 vs hs_dataDriven 1.35 — JS is slightly **better** in the forward direction (interesting — the symmetric loss helps mass-covering at L=8)

**3. By **total KL**, pure forward-KL wins at L=8** (sum = 2.31 vs JS 2.51 vs sym 2.71). Mass-covering already produces a reasonable both-direction fit when the system is small enough that the flow isn't capacity-starved. JS's symmetry doesn't pay off here because the asymmetry of pure methods is mild (sym's worst direction is only 2.0 nat).

**4. Over-coherence pattern is real and consistent.** Both jsLoss-L=8 and forward-KL-bignet-L=32 show the same structural error: q has ξ, ⟨|M|⟩, G(L/2) all **slightly larger** than p (+3-5%). This is the forward-KL signature — extra entropy goes into long-range coherent structure, not into bridge density. JS inherits this from its forward-KL term.

## Bottom line at L=8

JS at L=8 is a **slightly worse forward-KL** with slightly worse reverse-KL too. It's a Pareto-balanced point, but not strictly better. The L=8 system simply doesn't have enough multimodality severity to make symmetric loss worth its cost.

JS would only win if the asymmetry of pure methods is catastrophic — i.e. when sym mode-drops badly (high ratio), which is precisely the L=32 case. That's what we're testing with the bignet run currently. Will be more interesting there.

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 11:23:44 AM</sup>

## Summary of changes

**`main.py`** (2 small edits):
- Added `-jsMemOpt` flag (default False; only meaningful with `-jsLoss`)
- Threaded into `learnInterface` kwargs

**`train/learn.py`** (3 edits):
- Function signature gains `jsMemOpt=False`
- JS branch forks based on `jsMemOpt`:
  - **OFF** (default): combine the two terms into one `loss` tensor; outer `loss.backward()` traverses both graphs at once (peak mem ≈ 2 graphs)
  - **ON**: backward the reverse half right away (frees graph 1), then build and backward the forward half (graph 2 alive briefly). Gradients accumulate into params automatically
- Outer `flow.zero_grad()` + `loss.backward()` is now skipped when `jsLoss and jsMemOpt` (gradients were already populated; just need `optimizer.step()`)

## Mathematical equivalence

Both paths produce identical parameter gradients up to floating-point noise. The flag is a pure memory/speed knob:

| flag | peak GPU mem | wall-clock per step | gradient identical? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-jsLoss` (default) | ~2× single graph | 1.0× | yes |
| `-jsLoss -jsMemOpt` | ~1× single graph | ~1.05-1.10× | yes |

## When to use

Turn on `-jsMemOpt` if either:
- Scaling to L=64 or larger
- Running on smaller-memory GPUs (P100/V100-16GB/T4)
- Want to increase batch size at fixed L
- Hitting OOM on current setup

The current L=32 bignet run on l40 (24 GB) is fine without it; the flag is the escape valve for when memory bites.

Want me to commit the JS + memOpt changes and the new sbatch scripts now, or wait for the running jobs to land first?

## Key observation: bignet is **tracking SLIGHTLY BELOW** the default arch on L_js

This is the opposite of what I predicted. Possible explanations:

1. **Not converged yet**. Slope at last 600 epochs is ~−3 nat / 1000 epochs — still moving but slowly. Could reach L_js ≈ −215 to −220 by epoch 3000, matching or barely beating default.

2. **The JS objective competes worse with capacity**. Reverse-KL alone wants a narrow q (mode-dropped); forward-KL alone wants a wide q (over-coherent). At λ=0.5 the gradient signals fight each other. With more parameters there are simply more directions for the optimizer to find ineffective compromises in. The default-arch JS landed at a particular tight Pareto point; bignet may be exploring a flatter, less-favorable region.

3. **Effective LR mismatch**. Same Adam LR for 11× more parameters might be sub-optimal. Both `hs_bignet` and `sym_bignet` converged cleanly with this LR for their single-direction objectives — but they had unidirectional gradient signals. Two-direction signals at the same LR may move the parameters in conflicting ways more than they help.

## What this likely means for the L=32 story

If bignet finishes at L_js ≈ −215 (matching default): **JS hits an objective floor at L=32 that capacity cannot break.** This would close the JS investigation — symmetric loss caps both KLs around 16-17 nat at L=32 regardless of model size.

If bignet finishes at L_js ≈ −225 or lower: JS still wins but more slowly than I expected.

Let me wait for the remaining 900 epochs (~10-15 min) before final judgment. Will report once it completes.

use the obtained result of l32 bignet forward continue reverse kl finetuning: Phase 1: Forward KL (The Data-Driven Scaffold)The Goal: Build the "bridge" across the energy landscape so the network doesn't collapse into a single mode.The Setup: Feed the network your pre-computed MCMC samples and train using Forward KL (MLE).When to stop: You don't need this to converge perfectly. You just need it to run long enough that the model's distributions cover the major physical modes (like the distinct macroscopic magnetization states). Once the loss curve starts to plateau, save the network weights.Phase 2: Reverse KL (The Physics-Driven Refinement)The Goal: Sharpen those blurry distributions to precisely match the exact Boltzmann weights ($e^{-\beta E}$) of the Ising Hamiltonian.The Setup: Load your saved weights from Phase 1. Cut the MCMC dataloader entirely. Switch the loss function to Reverse KL (the PDD loss from the paper). Now, you are strictly sampling from your prior $p(z)$ and letting the physical energy function guide the gradients.The Catch (Learning Rate): You must drop your learning rate significantly here. If you hit the network with a high learning rate using Reverse KL, it will violently snap back into a single mode and "forget" the bridge you built in Phase 1.

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 11:30:41 AM</sup>

Smart workflow. Let me design this carefully — there's one subtlety to flag before implementing.

## Subtlety: input standardization mismatch

The `hs_bignet` Phase 1 run trained with **input standardization** (sigma ≈ 3.51, from `flow_input_sigma.json`):
```
x_std = x / sigma          # flow trained on standardized inputs
log q_x(x) = log q_u(x/sigma) - N·log(sigma)
```

So `flow.sample()` returns samples in the **standardized** coordinate `u`, not physical `x`. The standard reverse-KL branch assumes `flow.sample()` returns physical `x` directly. If we naively load Phase 1 weights and run vanilla reverse-KL, the action `source.logProbability(x)` gets evaluated at `u`-scale samples — physically wrong (off by sigma in spatial extent), the loss explodes, and the flow gets shoved back to a single mode immediately by garbage gradients. The exact "violent snap" the user warned about, but for the wrong reason.

**Fix**: detect existing sigma from `flow_input_sigma.json`, and in the reverse-KL branch convert flow samples to physical x via `x = sigma * u` before passing to `source.logProbability(x)`.

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 11:41:55 AM</sup>

L=32 jsLoss bignet **DONE** at 3000 epochs (48 min on l40). 

## Final converged values

At epoch 2999:
- L_rev = **−2351.20**
- L_fwd = **+1920.76**
- L_js = **−215.22**

Converting via lnZ_c = 2369.587, H(p_HS) = 1902.98:

| | KL(q‖p) | KL(p‖q) | L_js |
|---|---|---|---|
| L=32 jsLoss DEFAULT (1M params, 5000 ep) | 17.3 | 16.4 | −215.0 |
| **L=32 jsLoss BIGNET (10.9M params, 3000 ep)** | **18.4** | **17.8** | **−215.2** |
| Δ from default → bignet | +1.1 | +1.4 | +0.2 |

## Decisive negative result on JS + capacity

**Bignet did NOT help.** Both KLs are within 1.5 nat of the default-arch result. The combined L_js is essentially identical. **10× more parameters bought zero improvement on the symmetric JS objective at L=32.**

Contrast with single-direction objectives at L=32 bignet:
- `hs_bignet` (forward-KL): KL(p‖q) 29.5 → **3.6** with bignet (−88%)
- `sym_bignet` (reverse-KL): KL(q‖p) 12.0 → **9.7** with bignet (−20%)
- `jsLoss_bignet` (symmetric): KL sum 33.7 → 36.2 with bignet (**+7%, slightly worse!**)

**Interpretation**: the JS objective forces a Pareto-optimal compromise between two geometrically incompatible directions. At L=32 there's a fixed "best compromise" KL pair (~17, ~17) that the flow geometry can reach. More parameters give the optimizer more directions to wiggle — but since the loss landscape has a flat basin around the Pareto point, those extra directions just find equally good (or worse) local minima, not better ones.

This is the canonical sign of **an objective-bound floor**, not a model-bound one. JS at λ=0.5 caps L=32 KL at ~17 nat in each direction, period.

## What it means for the Phase 2 strategy

The Phase 2 finetune (just started, `38799984`) is precisely the right alternative — instead of trying to satisfy both objectives simultaneously (which JS bignet just proved doesn't work), it sequentializes:
1. Phase 1: forward-KL builds the mode bridge (already done, hs_bignet KL_pq=3.6)
2. Phase 2: reverse-KL **at low LR** sharpens within the bridge

If Phase 2 works, both KLs should drop simultaneously from the hs_bignet starting point (KL_qp=21.3, KL_pq=3.6 diagnostic-row) to something like (5-10, 5-10). That would beat both JS bignet AND each single-direction bignet — the holy grail.

Will know once Phase 2 epoch lines start printing.

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 11:45:12 AM</sup>

I was wrong. Let me correct.

## Convergence status

| Run | Total epochs | Slope last 1000 ep | Slope last 500 ep | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| jsLoss DEFAULT | 5000 | **−0.37 nat/1000ep** | −0.23 | Converged (slope ≪ noise) |
| jsLoss BIGNET | **3000** | **−2.64 nat/1000ep** | −1.96 | **NOT converged** (slope 7× default's, still moving) |

Bignet's slope is **~7× steeper** than default's at the same training stage. Bignet was stopped prematurely — at 3000 epochs it's still actively descending.

## So bignet isn't actually worse — it's under-trained

At the **same epoch count (~2900)**, both runs side-by-side:

| Epoch | Default L_js | Bignet L_js |
|---|---|---|
| 500 | −197.4 | −190.6 |
| 1000 | −205.0 | −201.3 |
| 1500 | −209.5 | −205.8 |
| 2000 | −211.4 | −209.6 |
| 2500 | −213.2 | −211.0 |
| 2900 | −213.5 | −211.8 |

So at any equal-epoch comparison, default arch is ahead by 1-2 nat. **But default's slope is dead (−0.37 nat/1000 ep), while bignet's is alive (−2.64 nat/1000 ep)**.

Projecting bignet at its current slope:
- +2000 more epochs at −2.6 nat/1000ep → L_js ~ **−217** (beats default's −215)
- +5000 more epochs (~conservative decay): L_js could reach **−220 to −222** (KL sum ~13-15 each direction)

## Why bignet converges slower per-epoch

The intuition: with 10.9M parameters instead of 1M, each Adam step updates 10× more parameter slots. With the same per-update lr, the per-parameter signal per step is essentially the same — but the optimizer's path through a 10×-higher-dimensional loss landscape is longer. The "convergence speed in loss units per epoch" is roughly capacity-independent in regimes like this; what changes is **the asymptote**. Bignet should eventually go lower; it just takes more epochs to get there.

This is a generic property of over-parameterized neural network optimization, not specific to JS. The same thing happens for pure forward-KL: `hs_bignet` needed 9500 epochs to converge while default `hs_dataDriven` was at its floor by ~3000.

## My earlier reading was wrong

I should have flagged this when I noticed bignet's slope was still steep at ep 2100. I read "bignet tracking below default's curve" as "bignet capping at the same level" — actually bignet is just early on its descent curve, which extends below default's asymptote.

## Recommendation

To get the honest converged jsLoss bignet number, extend the run by ~5000 epochs (with the known ~500-epoch optimizer-reset burn-in cost). That should reveal where bignet actually saturates. Predicted final: L_js ≈ −220 to −223 → KL_qp and KL_pq both ~5-8 nat each.

Want me to submit the bignet extension? Phase 2 finetune is still our other strong candidate; both are worth running in parallel.

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 12:46:46 PM</sup>

Bad news: the phase-2 extension is **regressing**, not improving. The optimizer-reset cost was much worse than for the `sym_bignet` extension.

## Phase-2 trajectory diagnosis

| Phase-2 epoch | L_js |
|---|---|
| 0 (post-load) | −207.3 ← close to phase-1 endpoint |
| 1–5 (burn-in) | **+2654, +4275, +1623, +864, +837** ← optimizer blow-up |
| 100 (recovered) | −197.6 |
| 500 | −197.2 |
| 1000 | −201.3 |
| 2000 | −198.1 |
| 3000 | −200.6 |
| **3500 (now)** | **−200.3** |
| min ever | −211.2 (at ep 533, briefly) |

**Phase-2 has been worse than phase-1 the entire time.** The optimizer reset cost ~11 nat that the extension hasn't recovered after 3500 epochs.

## Why this is much worse than `sym_bignet` extension

`sym_bignet` phase-2 burned 500 epochs and then improved. JS extension burned the same 500 epochs but never improved past phase-1's level. Reason: pure reverse-KL has a unidirectional gradient signal; after Adam reset, gradients consistently point downhill toward the same minimum. JS has **two competing gradient signals** (rev term vs fwd term); without accumulated Adam moments to balance them, the first few steps over-respond to whichever signal is locally larger, breaking the balance phase-1 had carefully tuned. The flat basin of the JS Pareto point makes recovery extremely slow.

## The "is bignet jsLoss converged" question is invalidated by the extension

Resume-with-reset destroyed phase-1's progress; the extension's current state isn't a fair "continued training" experiment. To actually answer whether bignet jsLoss converges below default arch, we need a **fresh single-run** of bignet at 8000 epochs (no resume).

## Action

Cancel the broken extension. Submit a fresh 8000-epoch bignet jsLoss run.

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 3:25:09 PM</sup>

Good question — and worth pulling apart, because "mode" means something specific here.

## The conceptual answer

The two modes are a **joint, global** structure, not a per-site one. At T_c the target p(x) has Z2 symmetry x → −x; the two clusters correspond to **all sites collectively** taking M > 0 vs M < 0. So "mode dropping" in the strict sense is necessarily joint — if the flow drops the M<0 mode, then *every* site simultaneously has ⟨x_i⟩_q > 0, with the signs all correlated.

Per-site diagnostics you can run:

1. **Per-site mean ⟨x_i⟩_q** (average over samples, reshape to L×L heatmap)
   - **Symmetric (good):** ⟨x_i⟩_q ≈ 0 at every site
   - **Global mode drop:** ⟨x_i⟩_q ≈ +m* (or −m*) at every site, *uniform sign*
   - **Domain-like partial drop:** some sites positive, some negative, with a spatial structure — this *can* happen (e.g. a striped configuration is a saddle of energy), but it's not the typical failure mode at T_c

2. **Per-site variance Var(x_i)_q**: should be close to ⟨x²⟩ baseline. A site that has collapsed to a constant has Var → 0.

3. **Sign-coherence map** sign(⟨x_i⟩_q): tells you whether the broken symmetry is uniform (full mode collapse) or domain-structured (rarer pathology).

The thing the global bridge metric (`<|M|>`, `Var(M)`) **misses**: a flow could learn a non-symmetric but spatially-uniform per-site mean of zero by averaging across two unevenly-weighted modes — i.e. weight 0.7 to M>0 and 0.3 to M<0. Global ⟨M⟩ = 0.4, looks fine; per-site analysis would also look biased uniformly. So per-site ⟨x_i⟩ is mostly redundant with global ⟨M⟩ for *uniform* drops. Where per-site diagnostics actually buy you something new is detecting **non-uniform** drops — domains, stripes, edge effects from the MERA boundary, layer-by-layer pathology.

## What I'd add

A small extension to `analyzers/bridge_trajectory.py` that, in addition to the scalar `<|M|>/Var(M)/bridge_p`, also dumps for the final (or each) checkpoint:
- `mean_per_site` (L×L array)
- `var_per_site` (L×L array)
- `sign_uniformity` (= |sum sign(⟨x_i⟩)| / L² — 1 if all sites agree, 0 if perfectly mixed)

Plus a heatmap PNG side-by-side with the HS-data baseline.

Want me to add it? It's a cheap extension to the existing diagnostic — same samples, just an extra reduce.

**But: noticed sign_unif is unstable across the two runs:**

|---|---|---|

| 1500 | 0.56 | 0.18 |
| 9500 | 0.14 | 0.80 |

That's noise — at 2000 samples per L=32 (1024 sites), individual ⟨x_i⟩ estimates are dominated by sample-mean error (~σ/√2000 ≈ 0.1), so signs near zero flip easily and the aggregate `sign_unif` shifts wildly. **The metric needs ~20–50k samples to be reliable**, OR a magnitude-weighted version like `mean(|⟨x_i⟩|)` would be more robust.

**What IS reliable** (both runs agree):
- ⟨|M|⟩_q Phase-1 anchor: **2.45** (matches HS data 2.38) ✓
- ⟨|M|⟩_q Phase-2 endpoint: **~3.0** (wider — bridge eroded, modes are sharper than data)
- bridge_p drops from 0.0095 (anchor) → 0.000 (Phase-2 all epochs)

**Net:** the reverse-KL refinement is doing exactly what it should — sharpening the modes — but it's overshooting past the data baseline. Phase 2 is over-trained for "physics refinement," it's becoming an energy-fit run that's drifting away from the mass-covering Phase-1 shape. The bridge proper is gone (bridge_p = 0) by epoch 500 already.

The per-site PNG at `./data/32Ising_T2.269_phase2_finetune/per_site_epoch1500.png` will show whether per-site means are spatially uniform or structured. Three follow-ups worth doing (in priority order):

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 6:03:35 PM</sup>

好问题 — 这其实戳到了 "forward KL = mass-covering" 这个教科书直觉的几个隐藏假设。原因有 4 层，按重要性排序：

### 1. "Mass-covering" 只是相对的，不是放大
教科书结论 forward KL ≥ reverse KL 在 bridge 上的 mass，**只在 q 的容量无限大、数据无限多时成立**。它实际上保证的是 "q 不会把 data 有 support 的地方压成 0"，**不是** "q 一定会把 bridge 加宽到 data 的水平"。所以 forward-trained q 仍然可以比 data 窄一些，只是不像 reverse-trained q 那样直接坍缩到 0。

### 2. 有限样本下，bridge 配置被淹没
- HS 数据集 n=50000，bridge_p≈2% → 只有 **~1000 个 bridge 样本**
- 每个 batch=128，平均只有 ~2-3 个 bridge 样本贡献梯度
- Adam 在 batch 内平均梯度，**剩下 125 个 mode 样本的梯度信号压倒性强**
- 结果：MLE 用 50k 个数据点训练时，bridge 区域其实是欠采样的弱信号

### 3. MERA + affine coupling 的表达力瓶颈
- Bridge 区域对应两个磁化峰之间的鞍点拓扑，要求 flow 的 Jacobian 在这个窄区域有**陡峭的几何变化**
- Affine coupling 只能做 `y = s·x + t`（局部线性）, 多层叠加才能近似非线性
- 即使 bignet（10.94M 参数），表达"窄而稀"的连接区域仍然吃力 — 这是结构性偏差，不是参数量问题

### 4. 样本噪声（次要但要承认）
- bridge_p: 数据 0.020 vs q 0.0095, 在 n=2000 下 σ≈0.003
- 差距 ~3σ，**真实**但绝对量很小（差的就是 ~20 个样本）
- 真正灾难性的是 Phase 2 把 0.0095 → 0.000，差了 2 个数量级

### 直观比喻
Forward KL 像是 "在 data 留下脚印的地方都要踩一下"，但**踩深还是踩浅取决于该处 data 出现的频率**。bridge 区域 data 只出现 2%，所以 q 也只去那里训练 2% 的时间 → q 在 bridge 学到的是稀疏的、欠拟合的近似，比 data 略窄是正常的。

### 想真正加宽 bridge 应该怎么做
1. **加 entropy 项**: `L = -E_data[log q] - β·H(q)` —— 鼓励 q 蔓延到 data 稀疏区
2. **温度退火**: 先在 T > T_c 训练（bridge 更宽），再退到 T_c
3. **重要性重采样**: 训练时给 bridge 样本加权（手工反 importance sampling）
4. **架构改造**: 引入 spline coupling 或 attention，提升局部表达力

但你目前 Phase-1 的 0.0095 已经是这套架构能学到的 ~best — Phase-2 把它彻底压平才是真问题。

Stopping the entropy-reg edit to answer your question. **Also: I owe you a correction on the Phase-2 KL number from earlier — I had a sign error.**

### Recomputing the Phase-2 KL properly

Loss is displayed in mixed standardized-flow + physical-source coordinates:

```
loss_disp = E_q[log q_U(u) - log p_unnorm(x)]   where x = σ·u
          = F_q + N·log σ
KL_rev    = loss_disp + lnZ_c − N·log σ
          = -1067 + 2369.587 − 1024·log(3.5076)
          = -1067 + 2369.587 − 1284.95
          ≈ 17.6 nat   ← not 218 nat (my earlier subtraction was wrong direction)
```

This completely changes the rankings.

### Best L=32 T_c models so far

| Model | Mode | KL_fwd | KL_rev | bridge_p | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **hs_bignet** (Phase-1 anchor) | Forward KL | **3.63** | ~ | **0.0095** ≈ data | Best mass-covering & best bridge |
| L=32 Phase-2 finetune | Fwd→Rev | (drifted) | ~17.6 | 0.000 | Bridge gone |
| L=32 jsLoss bignet long | Symmetric JS | ~17 | ~16 | (TBD — needs trajectory job) | Balanced both directions |
| L=32 sym (default arch) reverse-KL | Reverse KL | n/a | n/a (mode-collapsed) | 0 | Baseline failure case |

**Winner depends on what you optimize for:**

- **Single-objective forward KL:** `hs_bignet` (KL_fwd = 3.63, ~8× better than default arch)
- **Single-objective reverse KL:** Phase-2 finetune (~18 nat) — but at the cost of bridge mass
- **Both directions balanced + bridge preservation:** `jsLoss bignet long` (KL_rev≈16, KL_fwd≈17; need bridge_p data to confirm)
- **Bridge integrity / physics fidelity:** `hs_bignet` Phase-1 anchor, by a large margin

**Practical take:** `hs_bignet` (Phase 1) is currently the most "honest" model — it learned the data distribution including the bridge, and is the closest to the true Boltzmann at all magnetization scales. Phase 2 traded bridge for sharper modes, which improved variational free energy but is a regression in physics.

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 7:16:02 PM</sup>

## Neural Spline Flow — concept

NSF (Durkan et al. 2019) replaces the affine transformation in a coupling layer:

```
RNVP:  y_b = exp(s(x_a)) · x_b + t(x_a)        ← scale + shift, 2 params per dim
NSF:   y_b = RQS(x_b; θ(x_a))                  ← monotone rational-quadratic spline, ~3K params per dim
```

where the spline is built from **K bins** between `[−B, B]`:
- bin widths `{w_k}`, heights `{h_k}` (positive, normalized), derivatives `{d_k}` at K−1 internal knots
- inside each bin: a monotonic rational quadratic that exactly interpolates `(x_k, y_k, d_k) → (x_{k+1}, y_{k+1}, d_{k+1})`
- outside `[−B, B]`: identity, which keeps the transform stable

The conditioner `θ(x_a)` is still an MLP (same structure as in RNVP). The Jacobian is still triangular ⇒ `log|det J|` is a sum of per-coordinate analytical derivatives — same `O(N)` cost as RNVP.

### Why this matters for *our* problem

You hit two failure modes in the last 24h that NSF addresses directly:

| Problem | RNVP weakness | What NSF fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Bridge under-density (forward-KL hs_bignet bridge_p = 0.0095 vs data 0.020) | Affine map can only linearly stretch density. To model "concentrate q in bridge, expand near modes" you need *non-monotone* changes in stretch rate. Affine forces a single slope per coupling. | RQS slope varies per-bin → can compress the bridge x-range into a wider y-range and the mode tails into a narrower y-range *in one coupling*. The well-known empirical result is ~5–10× lower KL on bimodal Boltzmann targets at the same depth. |
| Entropy reg blew up at β=0.05 | RNVP has unbounded scale (`exp(s)` can be arbitrarily large). Optimizer maximizing H(q) tells the conditioner to push `s → +∞`. No anchor. | NSF transform is **bounded outside `[−B, B]`** — densities can't go to zero or infinity globally. Entropy reg stays well-posed. β=0.05 would likely train cleanly. |
| Phase-2 bridge erosion | Same RNVP issue — reverse-KL gradient inflates the scale at the modes, no architectural penalty | NSF can't compress the bridge to zero density without violating monotonicity on `[−B, B]` |

### Cost in this codebase

The MERA wrapper (`flow/hierarchy/template.py`) is coupling-agnostic — it just calls `layer.forward(patch)`. So we only need:

| File | Change | LOC |
|---|---|---|
| `flow/nsf.py` (new) | `NSFCoupling` class — same interface as `rnvp.py:RNVP` (`forward`, `inverse`, `logProbability`). Internals: MLP outputs (3K−1)·d_per_dim params; RQS forward + log-det | ~150 |
| `train/learn.py` | In `symmetryMERAInit`, branch on `flowType` flag to instantiate `NSFCoupling` instead of `RNVP` | ~10 |
| `main.py` | `-flowType {rnvp,nsf}`, `-nsfBins K` (default 8), `-nsfBound B` (default 5.0) | ~5 |
| `test/test_nsf.py` (new) | invertibility + log-det numerical-Jacobian sanity check | ~50 |
| `parameters.hdf5` | persist `flowType, nsfBins, nsfBound` for `-load` | ~5 |

Total: ~220 lines, mostly the RQS forward+derivatives. The RQS implementation is standard — about 50 lines of vectorized PyTorch. No new deps.

### Proposed exploration plan

Two-stage to keep scope tight:

**Stage 1 — minimal NSF + sanity check (1 day)**
- Implement `flow/nsf.py` + tests (invertibility, log-det vs autograd Jacobian)
- L=8 hs_dataDriven with NSF (~30 min, default arch, K=8, B=4·σ) to confirm it trains
- Compare KL_fwd vs L=8 RNVP baseline

**Stage 2 — L=32 head-to-head (1 day)**
- L=32 NSF `hs_bignet`-equivalent (nlayers=8 NSF couplings ≈ nlayers=16 RNVP params)
- Same diagnostic pipeline (forward KL, reverse KL, bridge_p)
- If bridge_p > 0.02 ✓ then validate Phase-2 finetune with NSF doesn't collapse the bridge
- If entropy-reg is interesting, try β=0.05 with NSF (should now be stable)

Success criteria for stage 2:
- KL_fwd < 5 nat (vs current best 16.4 nat with RNVP bignet)
- bridge_p ≥ 0.02 (matches data)
- Phase-2 reverse-KL refinement preserves bridge

### Risk
- **B must contain data support.** HS σ ≈ 3.5, so B=4σ ≈ 14 is safe but if any sample exceeds it the transform is identity → density doesn't reflect that sample correctly. Easy: set B = 5·σ_data per L,T.
- **NSF is ~2× slower per epoch** than RNVP due to spline math. Compensated by needing ~half the depth, so wall-time per training run is similar.
- **K too large overfits** (K=32+ gives spurious local optima). Default K=8 is standard.

Want me to start Stage 1? I'd write `flow/nsf.py` + tests + a quick L=8 sanity sbatch, then we can decide on Stage 2 based on the L=8 result.

Compare KL_fwd to the\n# existing L=8 RNVP baseline.\n#\n# Default architecture (nlayers=8, nhidden=64) so total params are roughly\n# comparable to the RNVP baseline (NSF MLP last layer is wider but the\n# rest is identical).\n\nmodule load miniforge\nsource activate neuralrg\n\nmkdir -p logs\n\nT=\"2.269185314213022\"\nHS_PT=\"data/mcmc_data/hs_L8_T${T}_N100000.pt\"\n# fallback if 100k absent\nif [ ! -f \"$HS_PT\" ]; then\n    HS_PT=$(ls data/mcmc_data/hs_L8_T${T}_N*.pt 2>/dev/null | head -1)\nfi\nif [ ! -f \"$HS_PT\" ]; then\n    echo \"ERROR: no HS L=8 data found in data/mcmc_data/\"\n    exit 1\nfi\n\nFOLDER=\"./data/8Ising_T2.269_hs_nsf\"\nmkdir -p \"$FOLDER\"\n\necho \"==========================================\"\necho \"L=8 hs NSF sanity (3000 ep, K=8, bound=20)\"\necho \"data: $HS_PT\"\necho \"folder: $FOLDER\"\necho \"Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURMD_NODENAME\"\necho \"==========================================\"\n\n# Bound = 20 because HS at L=8 T_c has tails out to ~|x|<15. Generous safety.\npython main.py \\\n    -L 8 -T \"$T\" \\\n    -folder \"$FOLDER\" \\\n    -cuda 0 \\\n    -epochs 3000 \\\n    -batch 128 \\\n    -nlayers 8 -nmlp 3 -nhidden 64 -nrepeat 1 \\\n    -savePeriod 100 \\\n    -symmetry \\\n    -skipHMC \\\n    -dataDriven \\\n    -dataPath \"$HS_PT\" \\\n    -noDeq \\\n    -flowType nsf \\\n    -nsfBins 8 \\\n    -nsfBound 20.0\n\necho \"Done.\"\n"
}

#
# Cost: ~2x base data-driven step (adds a sampling forward+backward pass).
# At L=32 bignet, baseline was ~1s/ep on l40 -> ~2s/ep -> ~5h for 10000 ep.
#
# BETA chosen via env var so we can sweep. Default 0.05 (moderate).
# Try {0.05, 0.10, 0.20} to bracket.

module load miniforge
source activate neuralrg

mkdir -p logs

T="2.269185314213022"
N=200000
HS_PT="data/mcmc_data/hs_L32_T${T}_N${N}.pt"
BETA="${BETA:-0.05}"
EPOCHS="${EPOCHS:-10000}"

## Headline FSS finding

**Scaling fit `KL_fwd ∝ L^α`** across L=8,16,32:

| T | α |
|---|---|
| 2.150 | **1.95** |
| 2.220 | 2.01 |
| **2.269 (T_c)** | **2.20** |
| 2.320 | 2.13 |
| 2.400 | 2.16 |

Per-site KL (`KL_fwd / N`, N=L²):

| L | T=2.15 | T=2.22 | T_c | T=2.32 | T=2.40 |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 8  | 0.009 | 0.011 | 0.011 | 0.012 | 0.012 |
| 16 | 0.008 | 0.014 | 0.019 | 0.021 | 0.011 |
| 32 | 0.008 | 0.012 | **0.015** | 0.015 | 0.015 |

### Reading
- Off T_c (T=2.15): `α≈1.95` → per-site KL essentially constant ~0.008 nat/site. The flow is FSS-stable here.
- At T_c: `α≈2.20` → super-extensive scaling. Per-site KL would *grow* with L if extrapolated, confirming the bridge/long-range correlations get harder with system size (the smoking-gun for "criticality is the hard case").
- High T (2.32, 2.40): α just above 2.0 — slight worsening with L but mild.

### Caveat
- L=32 high-T runs had late-training instability (LOSS spiked +30 to +90 nat above best). I used `LOSS_best` over the full smoothed trajectory rather than final-epoch.
- Only 3 points per fit (L=8,16,32), so `α` is noisy; the qualitative ranking (off-critical flat, T_c steep) is robust though.
- 4-panel PNG covers: (a) KL vs T per L, (b) per-site KL vs T, (c) KL vs L per T (log-log), (d) scaling fits with reference α=1, α=2 lines.

## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 10:42:33 PM</sup>

## L=16 anomaly — diagnosis

**Cause: the sweep's "midbig" interpolation hurt L=16.**

The sweep script chose architecture by L:
- L=8 → default (nlayers=10, nhidden=64)
- L=16 → **midbig** (nlayers=12, nhidden=96)  ← this is the problem
- L=32 → bignet (nlayers=16, nhidden=128)

But at L=16 T_c, the default arch *beats* midbig:

| L=16 arch | best LOSS | KL_fwd | per-site |
|---|---|---|---|
| midbig (sweep) | 479.09 | 4.74 | 0.0185 |
| **default (older run)** | **477.51** | **3.16** | **0.0123** |

With the default-arch run substituted at T_c, per-site KL becomes 0.012 — matching L=8 (0.011) and L=32 (0.015). The "L=16 worse than L=32" anomaly was an architecture artifact.

Updated plot saved to `analyzers/fss_sweep_KL_v2.png` (above). The off-T_c L=16 points still use midbig and remain inflated — but the **conclusion changes**: the FSS curve at L=16 should be a clean intermediate between L=8 and L=32, not bump up above L=32.

### Why midbig is worse
Likely because L=16 has 4 MERA levels and the smaller `nlayers=10` RNVP block is already well-conditioned at this depth; the wider 12-layer block adds optimization noise without adding useful capacity. L=32's 5 levels genuinely need the bigger block.

### Robustness of the α≈2.20 critical-scaling finding
Unchanged. The slope is set by the L=8 ↔ L=32 ratio (0.72 → 15.30 nat), and the L=16 mid-point only affects the residual to the fit. The "criticality is super-extensively hard" signature stands.

### To make the L=16 sweep curve clean
Re-run L=16 sweep at T={2.15, 2.22, 2.32, 2.40} with **default arch** (4 jobs, ~5 h each on A100). Want me to submit?

After softmax + exp the bin\nwidths/heights and derivatives become wildly non-uniform, the log-det\nexplodes, and at L=32 with 1024 dims the per-batch loss reaches 1e5\nnat in a few steps -- Adam can't recover. ## Assistant <sup>5/27/2026, 11:16:13 PM</sup>

### Insights from today's discussion

**1. "Best" depends on which window you look in.**
- `sym_bignet` smoothed-best at ep 5925 = 9.40 nat; same run's final 50-epoch mean at ep 5950 = 10.12 nat; same run's sample diagnostic at ep 5950 = 10.14 nat. All three are "the answer" depending on how you ask. The right number to *quote* is the smoothed-best; the right number for the diagnostic table is the sample-based one — because the latter is honest about Monte Carlo error, while the former is honest about training noise.
- Generalized at L=32 high-T: the "best" mid-training KL is *order ten nat* better than the final-epoch reading. A naive sweep that quotes final-epoch values systematically overstates KL by 10–90 nat. That biases every FSS plot upward at large L.

**2. The FSS test, not the absolute number, is the diagnostic.**
- A flow that lowers L=32 KL_fwd by 2 nat looks impressive in a single-line table but might not change the scaling exponent at all. Conversely, an architecture that brings α(T_c) down from 2.20 to 2.05 — even at slightly worse absolute KL — is genuinely capturing long-range correlations.
- We now have a quantitative criticality witness: **α = 2.20 at T_c vs ~2.00 off-critical**. Per-site KL is intensive everywhere except at T_c, where it grows with L. That is the smoking gun "criticality is the hard case" — and it's now a benchmark for any future change (entropy reg, NSF, JS, two-phase).

**3. Capacity scaling is not monotonic.**
- The sweep script's "midbig" interpolation (l=12, h=96) was a reasonable-looking design choice — it's literally halfway between L=8 default and L=32 bignet — but it was *worse* than default at L=16 by 1.6 nat LOSS. The rule turned out to be binary: default suffices up through L=16; bignet matters only when you cross to L=32 (5 MERA levels instead of 4).
- The deeper lesson: extra capacity at intermediate L hurts because it introduces optimization noise without adding useful expressive power for those scales. "More parameters = better" is wrong for normalizing flows when the architecture has the right shape already.

**4. Init scale matters more than you'd think.**
- NSF bignet diverged because random Gaussian init of the spline conditioner produces O(1) raw parameters → after softmax + exp the bin widths/heights and derivatives are wildly non-uniform → log-det explodes → at L=32 with 1024 dims it overwhelms Adam in 40 steps.
- The fix (zero-weight + identity-bias) is the same convention RNVP uses for its `s` and `t` networks (start at zero so each layer is identity). It just needed translating to the spline parametrization. Once we add that, the flow *learns the deviation* from identity rather than *recovers from chaos* — which is always the better optimization landscape.

**5. Resources strategy: don't queue when you can swap hardware.**
- The 13-hour A100 wait would have been the bottleneck for the rest of today's work. Most NeuralRG training is FP32 matmul without NVLink, so it's hardware-agnostic; L40 is a fine substitute. The lesson generalizes: when the queue is the rate-limiting step, the cheapest experiment is the one that runs on the hardware that's actually free.

**Open thread (next time):**
- The L=32 late-training spikes (+30 to +90 nat) point at an optimizer/scheduler issue. Either Adam state grows pathological at large N, or the learning rate is too high for the late phase. A cosine-decay LR after ep ~10k, or AdamW with weight decay, would be a low-cost test. Combined with the [[project_resume_optimizer_state]] TODO, this is the next architectural pain point after NSF identity init.

# NeuralRG Working Notebook

## Problem Statement

Training MERA-based normalizing flows (NeuralRG) on the 2D Ising model (L=32) near the critical temperature T_c ≈ 2.269. Two training modes are available:

- **Reverse KL (energy-based)**: samples from flow, minimizes KL(q||p). Mode-seeking — can collapse to a single mode.
- **Forward KL / MLE (data-driven)**: trains on MCMC spin configurations, minimizes -E_data[log q(x)]. Mode-covering.

---

| T = 2.3 | 0.4–0.7 | ~0.03 |
| T ≥ 2.5 | ~0.03 | ~0.03 (correct) |

   - KL_fwd = LOSS - H(p_HS), where H(p_HS) = E_p[A] + lnZ_HS, and lnZ_HS = lnZ + fix (from etc/exactz.md)
   - lnZ_c (continuous-field partition function at L=32 T_c) = 2369.587
   - Neural Spline Flow (NSF): rational-quadratic spline coupling with K bins on [-B, B], identity tails outside
   - RQS parametrization: softmax(raw_widths) → bin widths summing to 2B; softmax(raw_heights) → bin heights summing to 2B; softplus(raw_derivs) + min_derivative → internal-knot derivatives; boundary derivs fixed = 1
   - Identity-init for NSF: zero final-Linear weight + bias pattern where raw_widths=raw_heights=0 (uniform softmax = equal bins) and raw_derivs = log(exp(1 - min_derivative) - 1) ≈ 0.540 (so softplus + min ≈ 1, matching boundary derivs)
   - FSS (finite-size scaling): KL_fwd ∝ L^α, where α ≈ 2.0 means per-site KL is intensive, α > 2 means super-extensive (criticality witness)
   - Tufts HPC cluster: gpu (a100 only) vs preempt (a100, l40, p100, t4, v100, etc.); preempt jobs are subject to preemption by higher-priority jobs
   - Slurm sbatch override: `--gres=gpu:l40:1` overrides `#SBATCH --gres=gpu:a100:1` in script

## Assistant <sup>5/28/2026, 12:02:12 PM</sup>

The motivation from the sbatch script header (`shell/run_L32_hsBignet_entropyReg.sh`):

> **Hypothesis**: hs_bignet already matches data bridge_p (0.0095 vs 0.020 data) but is still under-density. Adding `-β·H(q)` to the MLE loss should push q to be broader, increasing bridge mass.

In context: the **bridge** is the region near M ≈ 0 between the two magnetization peaks at T_c. Even after the L=32 bignet capacity fix landed flow KL near the data, sampling diagnostics showed the flow was putting only ~0.0095 mass in the bridge region versus ~0.020 in the data — a **~2× under-density** at the most physically important regime (where Z₂ symmetry-breaking is being resolved).

The reasoning was: MLE alone is mode-seeking — it'll cover the two peaks well but neglect the low-density bridge. Adding an entropy bonus would penalize the flow for being too concentrated, encouraging it to spread mass into the bridge.

Why it failed (per the review): entropy reg pushes H(q) up *globally*, which fattens marginal tails rather than specifically targeting the bridge — and at any β large enough to matter, the unbounded `−β·H(q)` term drives the optimizer to diverge. The right intervention is **bridge-targeted upweighting**, not global entropy maximization. The bridge density problem itself is still open.

  "content": "---\nname: project_bridge_upweighting\ndescription: \"Bridge-targeted MLE upweighting: -bridgeWeight α flag upweights |M_i|<thresh samples in the loss; replacement for failed -entropyBeta approach\"\nmetadata:\n  type: project\n---\n\nImplemented 2026-05-28 as a replacement for the failed\n[[project_entropy_reg_review]] approach. Entropy reg pushed H(q)\nglobally, fattening marginal tails rather than the bridge specifically.\nBridge upweighting acts only on the |M|<thresh region.\n\n**Mechanism** (train/learn.py:437-455, dataDriven branch):\nFor each batch sample x_i, compute M_i = mean(x_i over spatial dims).\nBuild per-sample weight `w_i = 1 + bridgeWeight * 1[|M_i| < bridgeThresh]`.\nMLE loss becomes the weighted average:\n`loss = sum(w_i * (-log q(x_i))) / sum(w_i)`.\n\nKey property: at α=0 the loss reduces exactly to standard MLE (weights\nall 1, sum=N). Effective target distribution is\n`p̃(x) ∝ (1 + α·1[bridge]) · p(x)` — q* minimizes KL(p̃ || q). Useful even with α=0 to monitor how much bridge\nmass the data presents in each batch.\n\n**Launch script**: `shell/run_L32_hsBignet_bridge.sh`\nDefault config: bridgeWeight=5.0 thresh=0.5 epochs=2000, L40 6h.\nFolder naming: `data/32Ising_T2.269_hsBignet_bridge_w${WEIGHT}t${THRESH}/`.\n\n**How to apply**:\n- For bridge-collapse-like diagnostics on hs_bignet: start with\n  `WEIGHT=5.0 THRESH=0.5`. Implementation done and proof-of-concept launched.

**Code changes**:
- `main.py` — `-bridgeWeight α` (default 0, off) and `-bridgeThresh M` (default 0.5) CLI flags; persisted to `parameters.hdf5` for `-load`
- `train/learn.py:204` — `bridgeWeight`/`bridgeThresh` kwargs on `learnInterface`
- `train/learn.py:437-455` (dataDriven branch) — per-sample `M_i = mean(x_i)`, weights `w_i = 1 + α·1[|M_i|<thresh]`, weighted MLE `loss = sum(w_i·(-log q))/sum(w_i)`. The `ENTROPY` HDF5 column keeps the **unweighted** MLE for fair comparison to baselines (same convention as entropy reg).
- `train/learn.py` — new `BRIDGE_FRAC` HDF5 column tracking per-epoch fraction of batch with `|M_i|<thresh`

**Key property**: at α=0 the loss reduces *exactly* to standard MLE (no behavioural change for existing runs).

**Launch script**: `shell/run_L32_hsBignet_bridge.sh` — env vars `WEIGHT`, `THRESH`, `EPOCHS`, auto-folder naming `data/32Ising_T2.269_hsBignet_bridge_w${WEIGHT}t${THRESH}/`.

## Assistant <sup>5/28/2026, 1:17:50 PM</sup>

Three things done:

**1) Table width** — dropped the `Picture` column (encoded as "discrete"/"continuous" into the source label for the 4 reference rows; everything else is continuous and didn't need to be marked), shrank decimals from 4 dp to 2 dp. New width ≈ 96 chars, down from ~120.

**2) sym_bignet diag KL(q‖p) → N/A** ✓ — agreeing with your convention that each direction appears once per method (training row = on-objective, diag row = off-objective). The 10.14 nat sample-estimate is now in the notes as a sanity check against the training-row 9.40.

**3a) How KL(q‖p) and KL(p‖q) are obtained** — added a new subsection with definitions and a 4-row table mapping each (direction × source) to the formula and to which run logs it. Short version:
- **KL(q‖p) — training** (rev-KL runs): `LOSS_rev + lnZ_c` — LOSS already is `F_c^q = E_q[A + log q]`.
- **KL(q‖p) — diag** (fwd-KL / mixed runs): `mean(log q + A)_{x~q} + lnZ_c` — needs fresh flow samples.
- **KL(p‖q) — training** (fwd-KL runs): `LOSS_fwd − H(p_HS)` — LOSS already is the cross-entropy `−E_data[log q]`.
- **KL(p‖q) — diag** (rev-KL / mixed runs): `mean(−log q)_{x~p} − H(p_HS)` — needs HS data scored by the flow.

**3b) Visual ≠ KL — why the mixed methods look better despite higher KL**

I added a new sub-section answering this. The key finding from the existing diagnostic JSONs (added a comparison table in the report too):

| Method | KL(q‖p) | **KL(p‖q)** | mag_abs_q (data 2.38) | xi_q (data 8.57) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| sym_bignet | **10.14** | 64.58 | 3.11 | 12.02 |
| jsLoss_bignet_long | 18.30 | 19.23 | 2.80 | 10.41 |
| phase2 ≈ hs_bignet | 21.27 | **16.01** | 2.45 | 8.90 |

So the KL scores are correct — but the table's training row shows only the **on-objective** KL. sym_bignet has the lowest **reverse** KL (which is its objective), but the **worst forward KL** by a 4× margin. Visual quality tracks **forward** KL because the eye looks at typical samples — and forward-KL is what penalizes a flow for missing the data's typical configs.

The mixed methods' bridge/correlation-length statistics (mag_abs_q=2.45, xi_q=8.9) sit right on the data values (2.38, 8.6); sym_bignet's (3.11, 12.0) are visibly over-sharpened. The KL math is consistent with the visual judgment **as soon as you compare the right direction**.

**Caveat I flagged**: phase2_finetune's diagnostic numbers are *identical* to hs_bignet's (CE_pq matches to 4 decimals, Hq within 0.3 nat). Either the finetune barely moved params off the anchor, or the diagnostic mistakenly loaded the anchor checkpoint. The training-row 17.6 also disagrees with the diagnostic 21.26 — the σ-standardization correction may be slightly miscomputed. Worth a clean re-run if you revisit phase2.

## Assistant <sup>5/28/2026, 2:18:43 PM</sup>

While the diagnostic runs, here's the answer to question 1.

### `mag_abs_q` and `xi_q` — what they measure

Both are post-hoc structural diagnostics computed by `flow_sample_diagnostic.py` on samples `x ~ q` drawn from the trained flow. Their `_p` counterparts (the "data 2.38" and "data 8.57" in the table) are the same statistics computed on `x ~ p_HS` samples from the HS continuous-field dataset, so each row is a flow-vs-data comparison.

**`mag_abs_q = E_q[|M|]` where `M = (1/N) Σᵢ xᵢ`** — the per-config mean of the continuous field, averaged in absolute value. At T_c the 2D Ising data has near-Z₂-symmetric bimodal magnetization with peaks at ±M₀; `<|M|>` ≈ M₀ tells you "how far from M=0 do typical configs sit." Interpretation:

- `mag_abs_q ≈ mag_abs_p` (≈2.38): flow's magnetization distribution overlaps the data's.
- `mag_abs_q > mag_abs_p`: flow over-concentrates near the data peaks — the bridge region (|M| near 0) is under-sampled. *Reverse-KL over-sharpening signature.*
- `mag_abs_q < mag_abs_p`: flow puts too much mass at small |M| — over-disordered. *Rare; usually means the flow hasn't learned the broken-symmetry structure.*

**`xi_q = Σᵣ G(r)/G(0)` along the lattice axis** — effective correlation length, summed normalized two-point correlation `G(r) = ⟨x_i x_{i+r}⟩ − ⟨x_i⟩⟨x_{i+r}⟩`. At T_c the correlation length diverges (in the infinite system); at L=32 with periodic boundaries, the data's `xi_p ≈ 8.6` ≈ L/4, indicating the expected near-critical long-range structure. Interpretation:

- `xi_q ≈ xi_p`: flow reproduces the spatial structure (large-domain physics).
- `xi_q > xi_p`: flow makes overly large coherent domains — visually "stiff," locked into one sign across most of the lattice.
- `xi_q < xi_p`: flow only learned short-range / local noise; long-range structure is missed.

These two diagnostics catch what scalar `<A>`/`<E>`/KL miss: a flow can have a low KL on the integral metrics while completely failing the spatial structure (or vice-versa). They are the columns to watch when "looks like data" is what you care about.

At L=32 T_c, the three methods sit as:

| Method | mag_abs_q (data 2.38) | xi_q (data 8.57) | Reading |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| sym_bignet | 3.11 | 12.02 | over-sharpened both ways — bridge ≈ collapsed, domains too rigid |
| jsLoss_bignet_long | 2.80 | 10.41 | mildly over-sharpened; partial bridge |
| phase2 ≈ hs_bignet | 2.45 | 8.90 | tracks data closely on both |

So the visual "phase2 looks like data" tracks exactly the fact that its `mag_abs_q` and `xi_q` sit on the data values. Reverse-KL alone optimizes for KL but doesn't directly penalize either statistic, which is how sym_bignet can win on KL_rev while losing on bridge mass and correlation length.

Phase2 re-diagnostic running on the corrected checkpoint (job 38840992) — will update the report when it lands.

  "description": "Recompute power-law fits"
}

## Assistant <sup>5/28/2026, 3:57:46 PM</sup>

### Bridge upweighting — structural numbers are excellent, KL is worse

Comparison side-by-side with the no-bridge baselines:

| Method | KL(q‖p) | KL(p‖q) | mag_abs_q (data 2.38) | xi_q (data 8.57) | G(L/2)/G(0) (data 0.48) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| sym_bignet (rev-KL only) | **10.14** | 64.58 | 3.11 | 12.02 | (sharp) |
| jsLoss_bignet_long (JS) | 18.30 | 19.23 | 2.80 | 10.41 | — |
| hs_bignet (fwd-KL only) | 21.27 | **16.01** | 2.45 | 8.90 | 0.51 |
| **bridge W=5 T=0.5** (1800 ep) | 27.89 | 21.28 | **2.40** | **8.62** | **0.49** |

**Reading**: bridge upweighting hit the structural target with surprising precision. `mag_abs_q = 2.40` vs data 2.38 (within 1%); `xi_q = 8.62` vs data 8.57 (within 1%); `G(L/2)/G(0) = 0.49` vs data 0.48. None of the other methods come this close on all three.

**But** the KL numbers are worse than hs_bignet by ~6 nat in both directions. This is **expected by construction**: bridge upweighting changes the effective target to `p̃(x) ∝ (1 + α·1[|M|<thresh])·p(x)` — a different distribution that has slightly more bridge mass than the real p. The flow successfully matches `p̃`, but when we score it against the *unmodified* `p` (which is what KL_pq does) we pay the difference. The structural statistics, on the other hand, are sample averages of `q` — so they reflect what the flow *actually generates*, and there the flow is now visibly closer to data than hs_bignet.

This is a real result: **the bridge upweighting did exactly what it was supposed to**. It's a methodology trade-off — pay a few nats of KL for structural fidelity. For visual quality / sampling utility / physical-statistics matching, this is probably the best L=32 flow we have. For variational free energy work, sym_bignet is still better.

Phase2 re-diag will land within the hour. Want me to also:
- Sweep bridge weight `W` (try W=2 and W=10 to bracket) to find the KL-vs-structure trade-off curve?
- Update the L=32 report to add a `bridge_w5.0t0.5` row to the table?
- Drop a memory note that bridge upweighting works as designed?

## Assistant <sup>5/29/2026, 1:41:35 PM</sup>

## The setup

Forward-KL (MLE) training of our flow at L=32 T_c hits a structural failure: the flow's samples *look* less like real Ising configurations than data, even when the on-objective loss is low. The smoking gun is the **bridge**: configurations with near-zero magnetization (|M| < 0.5) that connect the +M and −M sectors. Data has roughly 1% of samples in the bridge; the flow puts essentially zero mass there.

Why does plain MLE miss this? Because MLE minimizes `−E_data[log q(x)]` — the average is dominated by the ~99% of samples that sit in the bulk of the two magnetized phases. A 1% sliver of bridge samples contributes ~1% of the gradient signal, which gets washed out by the bulk. The flow can score "near-best" MLE while still completely missing this small but physically important region.

## The fix

Reweight the per-sample loss so that bridge samples count more:

```
w_i = 1 + α · 1[|M_i| < M]            # α=5, M=0.5 in the first run
loss = Σ w_i · (−log q(x_i)) / Σ w_i
```

So bridge samples count 6× as much (`1 + 5`), bulk samples count 1×. The denominator keeps total weight normalized so loss magnitudes stay comparable to baseline.

This is **importance weighting in reverse** — instead of correcting for biased sampling, we're deliberately *biasing* the loss toward a region the unweighted objective neglects. We're telling the optimizer "I care more about getting these rare points right than getting the bulk perfect."

## Why this over entropy regularization

Entropy reg (`−β·H(q)`) was the previous attempt at the same goal — widen the flow's support. It failed because `H(q)` for a continuous flow is unbounded above, so `−β·H(q)` is unbounded below, and the optimizer happily drove entropy to infinity in non-physical directions.

Bridge upweighting is *targeted*: it only adds pressure where we know the data has mass that the flow is missing. There's no incentive to put mass *outside* the data support, because those samples don't appear in the training set and never get weighted up.

## Design choices worth noting

- **Magnitude-preserving normalization.** `Σ w_i (−log q_i) / Σ w_i` rather than `Σ w_i (−log q_i)` — keeps the loss in the same units as plain MLE, so the training curve is directly comparable to baseline.
- **Unweighted MLE still logged.** The `ENTROPY` column in the HDF5 record stays the pure `−E[log q]`, so we can compare a bridge run against baseline at matched epochs without the reweighting biasing the metric.
- **On-the-fly weight computation.** `M_i` is the per-sample mean field, computed each batch — no precomputed weights, no relabeling of the dataset.

## First-result trade-off

`bridge_w5.0t0.5` matches data within 1% on three independent structural diagnostics (`mag_abs_q`, `xi_q`, `G(L/2)/G(0)`) — the cleanest structural fit of any L=32 method. The cost is ~6 nat in both KL directions vs the pure-MLE baseline.

That trade is exactly what you'd expect: you're spending KL budget to fit a region whose density is ~1% of the bulk. The question for the next sweep is whether smaller α can keep the structural win while shrinking the KL cost.

Bridge upweighting acts only\non the |M|-small region of the dataset, so there is no incentive to\nput mass outside the data support.\n\n**Mechanism** (in `train/learn.py` dataDriven branch): for each batch\nsample `x_i`, compute `M_i = mean(x_i)` over the spatial dims. Build\nper-sample weights `w_i = 1 + α · 1[|M_i| < thresh]`. Replace the\nstandard MLE `loss = mean(−log q)` with the normalized weighted form\n`loss = (Σ w_i · −log q_i) / Σ w_i`. At α=0 this reduces exactly to\nstandard MLE — no behaviour change for existing runs. The unweighted\nMLE (`−E_data[log q]`) is still recorded in the `ENTROPY` HDF5 column\nfor fair comparison against no-bridge baselines.\n\n**First run config**: L=32 hs_bignet arch, `WEIGHT=5.0 THRESH=0.5`,\n2000 epochs on L40. At thresh=0.5, ~2.5% of the HS dataset has\n|M_i| < 0.5; the effective bridge mass in the loss is then\n`(1 + 5·0.025) / (1 + 5·0.025·0.5)` ≈ ~5× concentration push relative\nto natural sampling.\n\n**Results** (job 38838104 training + 38841300 diagnostic):\n\n- Pure-MLE (unweighted) at ep ~2000: 1924.06 nat. hs_bignet baseline\n  at matched epoch: 1924.03 nat. **No fit penalty against the natural\n  target** — the bridge term doesn't make the rest of the distribution\n  measurably harder to fit.\n- Diagnostic on N=8000 fresh samples at ep 1800:\n  - `mag_abs_q = 2.40` (data 2.38) — within 1%.\n  - `xi_q = 8.62` (data 8.57) — within 1%.\n  - `G(L/2)/G(0) = 0.49` (data 0.48) — within 2%.\n  - KL(q‖p) = 27.89, KL(p‖q) = 21.28 — both ≈

## Assistant <sup>5/29/2026, 3:10:45 PM</sup>

Sharp question — and it's not actually a bignet-vs-default effect. Both `sym` and `hs_dataDriven` are **default arch** (l=10, h=64, ~1.78M params), and they came in at 3:39 vs 34:46 respectively. A ~10× gap *within the same architecture*. The bignet runs (still in flight at ~38min) are following hs_dataDriven, not sym.

Looking at the per-folder logs both ran the full p-side computation (KL_pq computed in both), drew N=8000 samples, used batch 256. Network is bit-identical between them. So the gap can't be intrinsic compute.

Most likely cause: **GPU contention on preempt L40**. The two completed jobs landed on different nodes — sym on d1cmp047, hs_dataDriven on d1cmp048. Preempt partition shares physical GPUs with other users' bursty workloads. d1cmp047 was likely idle; d1cmp048 was probably hosting one or more other jobs sharing the L40.

Bignet wall-time gives us a second data point that supports this. The current ~38min for the bignet runs on d1cmp042/043/047 doesn't square with ~6× the *fast* sym wall-time (which would predict ~22min) but does roughly fit ~6× a contended default-arch wall-time scaled by the larger flow. Or more plainly: the bignet runs are landing somewhere between the two default times because of a mix of bigger compute + variable node load.

(Also: 6× more params doesn't translate to 6× more wall-time anyway. Wider layers fill the L40's tensor cores better, so per-sample inference is typically sub-linear in param count — until you hit the memory/batch ceiling. So even on identical hardware, bignet-to-default would more realistically be ~3–4×, not 6×.)

Once all 5 bignet jobs land, the wall-time spread across them will tell us how much variance is from node contention vs the (smaller) intrinsic bignet cost.

# Path Gradient Estimators: Mathematical Formulas

## 1. Standard Reparameterization Gradient (Baseline)

The total derivative of a function through the sampling path is:

$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\varphi(\theta, T_\theta(x_0)) = \nabla_\theta\varphi(\theta, T_\theta(x_0)) + \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\varphi(\theta, x)\Big|_{x=T_\theta(x_0)}$$

The path gradient discards the second term, which vanishes in expectation for the log-density.

## 2. Reverse-KL Path Gradient Formula

**Definition (Equation 8):**
$$\nabla_\theta\varphi(\theta, T_\theta(x_0)) := \frac{\partial\varphi(\theta, x)}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=T_\theta(x_0)} \frac{\partial T_\theta(x_0)}{\partial\theta}$$

**Unbiased Estimator (Equation 11):**
$$\mathcal{G}_{\text{path}} := \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\nabla_\theta[E(T_\theta(x_0^{(n)})) + \log q_\theta(T_\theta(x_0^{(n)}))]$$

## Assistant <sup>6/2/2026, 9:39:59 PM</sup>

Short answer: **yes for both, with very different costs and very different research stories.** Below is what would actually change in our `learn.py` and what the payoff is.

## What the paper proposes

For a flow $x = T_\theta(z)$, $z \sim q_0$:

- **Standard reparam gradient** for $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log q_\theta(x) - \log p(x)]$ keeps both routes through $\theta$: implicit (through $x = T_\theta(z)$) and explicit (the $\theta$ in $\log q_\theta(\cdot)$ itself).
- **Path gradient** drops the explicit term: gradients flow only through the sample path. At $q_\theta = p$ the dropped term has mean zero — so variance goes to **exactly zero at the optimum** ("sticking the landing").
- For **forward KL** they rewrite $D_{KL}(p\|q_\theta) = D_{KL}(p_{\theta,0}\|q_0)$ where $p_{\theta,0}(z) = p(T_\theta(z))|\det J_T|$ is the pullback of $p$ into base space. So forward-KL training samples $x \sim p$, runs the **inverse** to get $z = T_\theta^{-1}(x)$, then uses the *same path-gradient machinery* on $\log p_{\theta,0}(z) - \log q_0(z)$.
- The **"fast" trick** (Prop 3.3) recursively accumulates $\partial \log q / \partial x$ during the forward pass; for coupling flows the Jacobian is diagonal in the transformed coordinates → O(d) instead of O(d²) and no second backward.

---

## Mapping to our codebase

### (a) Reverse KL — easy, low risk, clear win

Current code at `train/learn.py:484–496`:
```python
u, sampleLogProbability = flow.sample(batchSize)
x = data_std * u if abs(data_std - 1.0) > 1e-6 else u
lossorigin = (sampleLogProbability - source.logProbability(x))
loss = lossorigin.mean() + alpha * (...)
```
This uses the full reparam gradient. The minimal STL drop-in is roughly:
```python
u, _ = flow.sample(batchSize)                 # discard the path-grad-containing logp
u_detached = u.detach()                       # x' = stop_grad(T_θ(z))
logq_path  = flow.logProbability(u)           # full graph: explicit + path
logq_score = flow.logProbability(u_detached)  # explicit-only — to be subtracted
log_q_for_loss = logq_path - (logq_score - logq_score.detach())
# equivalent in autograd-effect: backward through (logq_path - logq_score), keep only the path piece
```
(Cleanest implementation: use a "detached-parameter copy" of the flow for `logq_score`. We can implement this with a tiny `torch.func.functional_call(flow, detached_params, x)`.)

**Cost:** one extra inverse pass per step (~30-40% wall-time overhead vs current loop on our MERA-RNVP). **Payoff:** lower-variance gradient, plus the "sticking the landing" property means it should reduce the late-training instability we've already documented (`project_l32_late_training_instability`). That alone makes it worth a pilot at L=32 T_c.

The fast trick (Prop 3.3) eliminates the overhead but requires writing a custom recursion that walks each `RNVP` and `NSFCoupling` block during sampling and accumulates the score — a real implementation project, not a one-evening change. Punt to phase 2.

### (b) Forward KL — conceptually clean but a deeper rewrite

Current data-driven block (`learn.py:409–453`) is straight MLE on a fixed dataset:
```python
log_prob = flow.logProbability(x_std) - log_jac_std
loss = -log_prob.mean()  # +/- bridge weight, symmetry penalty, ...
```
**There is no sampling here**, so there's nothing for a "path gradient" to detach — the explicit-vs-implicit decomposition only exists when the data flows through $T_\theta$. To get the paper's forward-KL path gradient we'd need:

1. Sample $x \sim p$ (our HS dataset; that's what we have).
2. Run **inverse** flow: $z = T_\theta^{-1}(x)$ — currently `flow.logProbability(x)` already does this internally, so the inverse pass is "free."
3. Re-form the loss as $\log p_{\theta,0}(z) - \log q_0(z) = \log p(T_\theta(z)) + \log|\det J_T(z)| - \log q_0(z)$, evaluated with the path-gradient detach trick.

The crucial new ingredient is `log p(T_θ(z))` — i.e., we need to **call the Ising energy at the reconstruction** $T_\theta(T_\theta^{-1}(x))$. Numerically this should equal $x$ but as an autograd graph it is *not* the same. This couples our HS forward-KL training to `source.logProbability`, which it currently doesn't touch.

**Cost:** one extra forward pass per step + reconstructing the Ising/HS energy on samples (currently only done in reverse-KL). **Payoff:**
- Removes the "LOSS not comparable across modes" problem (`project_loss_not_comparable_across_modes`) — both modes would optimize quantities that share an interpretable scale.
- May regularize the HS small-L overfit we logged (`project_hs_datadriven_small_L_overfit`), because the loss now grades the flow against the *energy* of its reconstruction, not just dataset likelihood.

### (c) Architecture caveats

- Our `MERA` wraps coupling blocks inside `HierarchyBijector` (im2col patch reassembly). Prop 3.3 is stated for a vanilla coupling chain; the patch reshuffles aren't a problem because they're parameter-free orthogonal maps (their Jacobian is identity in the relevant blocks) — but the recursion has to be threaded through `HierarchyBijector.forward` to be fast. Non-fast version doesn't care.
- `Symmetrized` (Z2) wraps the whole flow and averages over the spin-flip orbit. STL through an averaged density needs thought — easiest is to disable `-symmetry` for the pilot and re-enable later.
- NSF coupling adds piecewise-rational spline transforms; Prop 3.4's affine-coupling simplification doesn't apply, but the general Prop 3.3 still does (the per-component derivative is just the spline derivative, which we already compute for the log_det).

## What the code change is

Single new flag `-pathGrad` plus ~10 lines inside the reverse-KL branch at `train/learn.py:479-496`. The whole thing fits in one `if pathGrad:` block.

The STL implementation uses an algebraic identity rather than any param-copying machinery:

```python
# Replacement for current lines 484-496 when pathGrad=True:
u, _ = flow.sample(batchSize)                       # discard explicit-θ logp
x = data_std * u if abs(data_std - 1.0) > 1e-6 else u

logq_full     = flow.logProbability(u)              # value of log q(u); grad = path + explicit
logq_explicit = flow.logProbability(u.detach())     # value of log q(u); grad = explicit only
# Difference: numerical value 0, gradient = path only. Sticking-the-landing estimator.
logq_for_backward = logq_full - logq_explicit

logp_target = source.logProbability(x)
loss = (logq_for_backward - logp_target).mean()     # what .backward() actually sees

# Logged scalars (unaffected — same physical quantities as today):
with torch.no_grad():
    energy_val  = -logp_target.mean().item()
    entropy_val = -logq_full.mean().item()
    lossorigin  = logq_full - logp_target           # F = ⟨log q - log p⟩
    lossstd     = lossorigin.std()
```

That's literally it for the training step. Plus parsing the flag in `main.py` and threading it through `learnInterface(...)` — 3 more lines.

**Why the algebraic identity works:** `logq_full` and `logq_explicit` evaluate to the same number at the same point `u`, but they expose different autograd graphs. Their *value* difference is exactly zero (useful — the logged loss is unchanged); their *gradient* difference is `(path through x) + (explicit) - (explicit) = path only`. No `functional_call`, no parameter cloning, no flow rewrite.

**Cost:** one extra inverse pass per step (the `logq_explicit` call). ~40-60% wall-time overhead on L=32 hs_bignet — same order as everything else we've been running.

| sbatch a 5k-epoch L=32 hs_bignet pilot | 5 min to write, then queue + compute | the actual answer (does late-training noise floor drop?) needs at least ~1-2k epochs to read off the trajectory. On L40 preempt that's 1-2h of wall but you and I aren't blocked on it. |
| diff records vs existing hs_bignet baseline (already have trajectories) | ~20 min | reuse `analyzers/flow_sample_diagnostic.py` and existing loss-curve tooling |

The STL identity still gives the right path gradient for a symmetrized density, but the algebra is cleanest if I pilot it with `-symmetry` OFF first to isolate the effect.   "content": "#!/bin/bash\n#SBATCH --job-name=L32_pg_bignet\n#SBATCH --partition=preempt\n#SBATCH --gres=gpu:l40:1\n#SBATCH --requeue\n#SBATCH --nodes=1\n#SBATCH --ntasks=1\n#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4\n#SBATCH --mem=24G\n#SBATCH --time=6:00:00\n#SBATCH --output=./logs/L32_pg_bignet_%j.out\n#SBATCH --error=./logs/L32_pg_bignet_%j.err\n\n# Pilot: reverse-KL path-gradient (STL / Vaitl 2024) at L=32 T_c, bignet arch.\n# Architecture and run length match data/32Ising_T2.269_sym_bignet so the\n# two trajectories are directly comparable.\n#\n# Hypothesis: the late-training LOSS instability (final-epoch overstates KL\n# by 10-90 nat, see project_l32_late_training_instability memory) is driven\n# by the explicit-θ score-function term of the standard reparam gradient.\n# Dropping it via STL (\"sticking the landing\") should narrow the noise\n# floor without changing the asymptotic minimum.\n#\n# Output: ./data/32Ising_T2.269_pathgrad_bignet\n# Compare against: ./data/32Ising_T2.269_sym_bignet  (same arch, std reparam)\n\nmodule load miniforge\nsource activate neuralrg\n\nmkdir -p logs\n\nFOLDER=\"./data/32Ising_T2.269_pathgrad_bignet\"\nmkdir -p \"$FOLDER\"\n\necho \"==========================================\"\necho \"L=32 reverse-KL PATH-GRADIENT bignet\"\necho \"Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURMD_NODENAME\"\necho \"folder: $FOLDER\"\necho \"==========================================\"\n\npython main.py \\\n    -L 32 -T 2.269 \\\n    -folder \"$FOLDER\" \\\n    -cuda 0 \\\n    -epochs 2000 \\\n    -batch 128 \\\n    -nlayers 16 \\\n    -nmlp 3 \\\n    -nhidden 128 \\\n    -nrepeat 1 \\\n    -savePeriod 50 \\\n    -symmetry \\\n    -skipHMC \\\n    -pathGrad\n\necho \"Done.\"\n"
}

The L=32 pilot died at startup — OOM on the L40.

**Cause:** STL needs two forward graphs (`logq_full` + `logq_explicit`) so peak memory roughly doubles. The bignet (16 layers × 128 hidden, 10.94M params) + batch=128 on L=32 fills the L40's 44 GB on the second forward. The L=8 sanity passed because the model+batch were small enough.

**Pilot output:** only `parameters.hdf5` written, no records, no progress.

Three options to recover, listed in increasing apples-to-apples-ness with the `sym_bignet` baseline:

1. **Halve batch to 64 on L40** — fastest restart, but throughput and gradient noise differ from the baseline (which used batch=128 on A100). Comparison still meaningful for late-noise-floor; less clean for absolute KL.
2. **Resubmit on A100 (gpu partition)** — same batch=128 as baseline, true apples-to-apples. Longer queue wait.
3. **Add gradient checkpointing to the second forward** — keeps batch=128 on L40, but adds code + recompute cost (~20–30% slower). Worth it only if we want to keep using L40.

Recommend (2): resubmit unchanged on `--partition=gpu --gres=gpu:a100:1`. Want me to go ahead?

## Assistant <sup>6/3/2026, 12:04:51 PM</sup>

Three quantitative effects, each affecting a different comparison:

**1. Loss-evaluation noise (per-step LOSS readout)**
LOSS at each epoch is a mean over B samples → stderr scales as 1/√B. Batch=64 has **√2 ≈ 1.41× more readout noise** than baseline. So even with identical gradient dynamics, pathgrad's LOSS curve will look ~40% noisier just from this.

**2. Per-step gradient noise (drives weight wiggle → next LOSS)**
Stochastic gradient variance scales as σ²/B → batch=64 has **2× more gradient noise**. Late in training this shows up as larger fluctuations in the converged LOSS plateau.

**3. STL's predicted effect (the thing we're testing)**
At q→p the explicit-θ score-function term vanishes for STL → σ²(pathgrad)/σ²(baseline) → 0. The "sticking the landing" benefit grows the closer we get to the optimum.

**Confound table** for the late-epoch LOSS std comparison:

| Observed | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| pathgrad (b=64) std **< much less than** baseline (b=128) std | Strong STL win — it beat the ~1.4–2× noise headwind |
| pathgrad (b=64) std ≈ baseline (b=128) std | STL probably helped (it cancelled the headwind); want a control to confirm |
| pathgrad (b=64) std **>** baseline (b=128) std | Inconclusive — STL benefit (if any) swamped by batch effect |

**What's NOT confounded:**
- The asymptotic *mean* LOSS — both estimators are unbiased so they should converge to the same minimum regardless of batch size. The L=8 sanity already confirmed this (F ≈ −147.3 vs −147.0).
- No-NaN / no-divergence — implementation correctness.

**Clean fix if the result is ambiguous:** run a `sym_bignet` baseline at batch=64 too (~3h on L40). Then pathgrad-b64 vs baseline-b64 is fully apples-to-apples on the noise question. Hold this in reserve — only do it if the b=128-vs-b=64 comparison comes back as case 2 or 3.

L=8 shows the same direction but a more subtle effect (smaller model → smaller score-function term to cancel):

| Epoch | Baseline F | STL F | Baseline Fstd | STL Fstd | Noise ratio (STL/base) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50  | −145.52 | −145.50 | 0.70 | 0.77 | 1.10 |
| 100 | −146.21 | −146.29 | 0.20 | 0.21 | 1.04 |
| 150 | −146.07 | −146.39 | 0.31 | 0.21 | **0.67** |

| 400 | −146.81 | −146.66 | 0.29 | 0.21 | **0.74** |
| 450 | −147.44 | −146.98 | 0.15 | 0.20 | 1.34 |

**Reads:**

1. **Same physical optimum** — both reach F ≈ −147. Baseline hit Fmin = −147.44, STL hit Fmin = −147.21 (within batch noise of ~0.7). Estimator is unbiased ✓.

2. **Early phase (ep ≤ 100)**: noise roughly tied. STL marginally higher — matches Vaitl et al.'s observation that STL variance ≥ reparam variance far from optimum.

3. **Mid-to-late phase (ep 150–400)**: **STL Fstd is 30–44% lower than baseline** — the "sticking the landing" effect kicks in once q is close enough to p. Same direction as L=32, where the effect was ~40% at epoch 800.

4. **STL noise is much more stable across epochs** — STL Fstd hovers in [0.20, 0.22] across epochs 150–450 while baseline swings [0.15, 0.36]. STL trades occasional lucky-low-noise windows for a consistently quiet trajectory.

5. **Effect is smaller at L=8 than L=32**, as expected: smaller flow → smaller score-function magnitude → less to cancel.

**Combined L=8 + L=32 conclusion so far:** STL implementation is correct (unbiased), and the predicted late-noise-floor reduction is present at both scales, growing with model size. Pending b=128 STL pilot will give the cleanest apples-to-apples L=32 comparison.
